other_side: Zitron, writing two days later in a paid piece of which only the opening is free to read, welcomes the result and says the blue wave could burst the bubble. He argues the bubble's supposed inevitability rested on the assumption that the rich and powerful always get what they want, and that its backers never expected voters to say no. Nvidia's growth depends on an unimpeded build-out, he says, and without more capacity the labs cannot sell a story of endless growth; once that sets in, "everything begins to implode".
truth_beneath: The variable both men orbit is whether local consent merely raises the price of building data centres or actually stops them. Both accept as fact that voters punished candidates who backed local data centres, that ballot measures passed almost everywhere, and that developers spent years ignoring communities. The empirical question is whether new governors set conditions or impose lasting pauses; the observable is construction starts and permits in Texas and Ohio over the next three quarters. The residue is worldview: whether the build-out is useful infrastructure owed a fair bargain, or speculative excess that deserves stopping. For Whittemore to be vindicated, governors must set hard but achievable rules and building must continue. For Zitron, moratoria must stick, capacity stall and lenders withdraw. Both are polemicists with incentives: Whittemore bullish and anti-doom, Zitron bubble-certain and anti-hype. The signal is their agreement that the industry lost the public and cannot build without consent again. Watch what Texas's new governor does on taking office in January.
